TextView.android:text: Advanced Lesson 18: Pigeonhole and Dirichlet's Principle

The Pigeonhole Principle is the most fundamental tool in combinatorics. It states that if you have n items and you put them into k boxes, where n > k, then at least one box MUST contain more than one item. While it sounds incredibly simple, this principle is the key to proving some of the most deep and complex theorems in mathematics. It is also known as Dirichlet's Principle.

The true power of this principle is revealed in existence proofs. Often in math, we cannot easily construct an object that satisfies a property. Instead, we can use the Pigeonhole Principle to show that it is mathematically IMPOSSIBLE for such an object NOT to exist. If you have enough pigeons and enough holes, the collision is inevitable. This simple logical leap is the engine behind huge sections of Ramsey Theory and Extremal Graph Theory.

There is a generalized form of the principle: If you distribute n items into k boxes, then at least one box contains at least ceil(n/k) items. This is extremely useful for optimization problems. The principle is not restricted to finite sets, but its application there is most direct. It is used in everything from finding rational approximations of real numbers to proofs about scheduling and computer science.
Prove that if you pick 10 numbers from 1 to 20, at least two of them must have a sum of 21.

Solution: We use the Pigeonhole Principle. Consider pairs of numbers that sum to 21: (1, 20), (2, 19), (3, 18), (4, 17), (5, 16), (6, 15), (7, 14), (8, 13), (9, 12), (10, 11). There are exactly 10 such pairs. We have 20 numbers total, partitioned into 10 disjoint pairs. If we choose 10 numbers from 1 to 20, we have chosen 10 'pigeons'. If we treat these 10 pairs as our 10 'holes', and we pick 10 numbers, it is possible to pick one from each pair and avoid a sum of 21. BUT, if we were to pick 11 numbers, we would necessarily pick both numbers from at least one pair! Actually, the problem asks to prove it for picking 11 numbers. The principle shows that choosing 11 numbers forces a pair. Proof complete.
